items.title: Greg Caputo interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 14, 1998
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...it seems like there’s a healthy group of fairly young musicians who are keeping the let’s say mainstream tradition alive, kind of a little resurgence with Scott Hamilton there...

ctx.x: I have a friend who’s a drummer. He happens to be a person of color, and I don’t even like to say that to be honest with you because I look at people as people and I’ve never met a man I don’t like, Will Rogers. It’s however they act and treat me that will judge that in the end. But I’ve been in situations where I’ve gone to clubs that were predominantly black and I just don’t have that attitude so they don’t give me that attitude. My friend is a person of color and he’s like one of my best friends. And we share…

From what I’ve been able to observe it seems like there’s a healthy group of fairly young musicians who are keeping the let’s say mainstream tradition alive, kind of a little resurgence with Scott Hamilton there, but it doesn’t seem like there’s as many young black musicians who are embracing that style, that they seem to be devoted more towards really kind of modern.

Well we could talk about that. I think that what you’re saying is partially true about them keeping the roots of bebop alive, but I hear experimentation from some younger players, I mean get into that. Maybe what they’re coming up with isn’t commercially viable or marketable and so we don’t really hear it. But as far as experimentation going on, certainly. But whether we can get record producers to get it out there is a big problem, and we may not be hearing some of the next steps to jazz or to modern music to…
